claims.text: High-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings resist time-dependent plastic deformation.
Nanoscale interfaces act as significant barriers to dislocation motion.
Dislocations pile up at nanoscale interfaces.
Interface-induced dislocation pile-ups delay creep onset.
The proposed coatings consist of alternating high-entropy-alloy layers with nanoscale thicknesses.
The initial coating microstructure is predominantly defect-free at room temperature.
Reducing the multilayer period while holding overall composition constant increases interface density.
Creep is to be evaluated under sustained mechanical loading at controlled temperatures below the onset of significant diffusion-driven processes.
A high density of mismatched interfaces impedes cooperative dislocation motion.
Impeded cooperative dislocation motion delays the initiation of plastic deformation under sustained stress.
Impeded cooperative dislocation motion reduces the rate of plastic deformation under sustained stress.
Finer multilayers are expected to have lower steady-state creep rates than thicker multilayers.
Finer multilayers are expected to have lower steady-state creep rates than single-phase high-entropy-alloy coatings.
Finer multilayers are expected to exhibit less time-dependent plastic deformation than thicker multilayers or single-phase high-entropy-alloy coatings.
The interface-barrier mechanism is expected to dominate at low temperatures where diffusion is limited and phase stability is maintained.
The proposed mechanism applies when layer thickness remains in the nanoscale regime.
Microstructural heterogeneity and experimental variability may affect the magnitude and statistical significance of creep-rate reduction.
Failure to observe a statistically significant creep-rate reduction at higher interface density relative to both controls would falsify interface barriers as the primary cause.
